methodological_questions: Does adherence to the recommended mix predict game or series wins beyond team quality?
Is the recommendation or adherence label derived from the same outcomes (points per possession) it is used to predict?
Is a sample of 54 series enough power?
How should team quality and opponent strength be controlled?
Is play-type tagging reliable enough, given tagger floors and the large INSUFF share?

historical_evidence.finding: Series-level AVOID share vs winning: game-level rho=-0.19 p=0.008 (inflated n, team-quality confound); series-level rho=-0.26 p=0.07 (n=50, underpowered; ~80 series stated as needed for p<0.05). Low AVOID-share bin 52.6% win vs 25-50% bin 37.0%. Still confounded by team quality (OKC disciplined and good). Verdict recorded: inconclusive.

Descriptive conformance of observed mix vs recommended opener in 4 playoff G1s (8 offense sides). Average |delta| 4.5pp to 24.0pp on leverage buckets; 4 of 8 sides best matched opener #3, not rank-1. CUT and PNR muted by tagger floor; single-game horizon; no outcome comparison.

LLM counter selection vs deterministic BEST tier: n=3 triggers, agreed with BEST 1/3, picked AVOID 2/3. Mean H2 PPP was BEST 1.650, agent 1.154, AVOID 0.642. Caveat: 230+ disagreements needed. Verdict recorded: inconclusive.

Season adapter profiles, 19 teams with at least 2 seasons. BEST share varies by team (BOS 15.7%, win 70%; HOU 2.5%), but win% does not line up with BEST share (IND 4.5% BEST, 71% win; DEN 4.9% BEST, 70.8% INSUFF, 62% win; ORL AVOID 59.3%, 0% win). No inferential test of stability vs noise.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Series-level association of AVOID share with winning (n=50) as evidence of a mix effect independent of team quality
failed_approaches.why: A_unanswerable: underpowered (p=0.07) and still confounded by team quality (LIM:small_sample, LIM:confounding).
Inflated n and team-quality confound; the p=0.008 is not interpretable as an independent effect.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Testing BEST-tier counter choice against alternatives on n=3 triggers
Using single-game conformance to the recommended opener as an adherence measure
failed_approaches.why: E_unclear: mechanical floor (CUT and PNR muted by tagger floor), single-game horizon, no outcome comparison.

evidence_establishes: A closely related series-level test (AVOID share vs winning, n=50) was recorded as inconclusive: the direction is negative (rho=-0.26, p=0.07), not significant, and confounded by team quality.
Game-level association exists but is inflated by n and team quality, per the record.
Observed adherence to the recommended mix is often partial and varies widely (4.5pp to 24.0pp average gap in a descriptive sample).
Descriptive team-level BEST share does not map cleanly onto win% (FAM:SF08).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether adherence to the recommended mix predicts winning independent of team quality.
Whether the recommendation is out-of-sample or derived from outcomes, since no retrieved record validates it (all validation statuses are no_validation_recorded).
Whether adherence is reliably measured across seasons and play types given tagger floors and large INSUFF shares.
own_inferences: With 54 series, the previously seen rho of about -0.26 would give a p-value near 0.05 and power well under 80% (roughly 50%); 80% power would need on the order of 110 series. This is my own calculation, not a recorded figure.
Adding 4 series to the n=50 analysis barely changes the power picture, so 54 series alone will likely reproduce an ambiguous result.
If recommended tiers are defined by post-trigger points per possession, adherence correlates mechanically with scoring and hence winning, which creates an outcome-derived-label artifact risk.

A within-series, game-level design with team or series fixed effects could use more units while controlling team quality, but only if adherence varies across games within series and is measured reliably.
The question as posed is closer to an extension of the AVOID-share study than a new question, so a stronger adherence measure plus confound control is the only added value.
uncertainties: How adherence is operationalised (BEST share, AVOID share, distance to recommended mix) and over what window is not specified.
Whether the recommended mix was built from the same seasons it will be tested on.
The share of possessions classified INSUFF per series, and the number of suppression triggers per series, are unknown.

The 54-series count versus the full set of available series is unclear. The 2025-26 playoffs were partial on the question date and complete only from 2026-06-21, so results may depend on the data version.
Tagger reliability by play type across the four seasons is not documented in the retrieved records.

historical_effect.explanation: Without prior records I might have run the series-level correlation directly. The retrieved record of the same design (n=50, p=0.07, confounded, inconclusive) shifted the decision to require changes: confound control, an out-of-sample recommendation definition, a within-series design, and a pre-specified inconclusive outcome if power is lacking.

methodological_questions: Does adherence to a recommended play-type mix predict game or series wins?
Is the recommended mix derived from the same outcomes it is tested against (outcome-derived label, leakage)?
Is a sample of 54 series enough power to detect an adherence effect?
How should confounding by team quality and opponent be handled?
How reliable is play-type classification and suppression estimation across seasons?
args.query: adherence to suppression-conditional recommended play-type mix predicts winning; best/avoid counter strategy against defensive suppression; series-level test with 54 series

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Returns the most relevant consolidated study-family records of earlier research by this project that are available in this setting, with their identifiers; returns an empty list when none are available.
- glossary(): definitions of basketball and project terms used in task statements.
- data_catalog(): the fields available in each per-game data file.
- search_documents(query): rank further study-family documents by text relevance; returns up to 4 families not yet returned.
- read_family(id): the complete record of one study family (for example 'FAM:SF-APPA-001').

Protocol: every reply is exactly one JSON object and nothing else.
To call a tool: {"action": "tool", "tool": "<name>", "args": {...}}
To finish (stage 2 only): {"action": "final", "output": <object following the stage-2 schema>}
You may call at most 12 tools; then you must finish. Check that every opening brace has a closing brace.

Risk codes (use only these): SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER, EXPOSURE_SPARSITY, MEASURE_RELIABILITY, RTM_SELECTION, OUTCOME_DERIVED_LABEL, LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD, MECHANICAL_FLOOR, BASE_RATE, CONFOUNDING, LABEL_ERROR, PLACEBO_DEPENDENCE, MULTIPLE_TESTING, IMPLEMENTATION_BUG, DRIFT_NONSTATIONARITY

Research question (as posed on 2026-06-16, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

reasoning_details.text:
I'm weighing whether to pull up the full SF-CHT-039 file or run another search, but I've got enough budget and can likely wrap up without it. The core question is whether sticking to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning across the 54 series. The prior study on 50 series showed a weak, non-significant negative link for AVOID share, so I'd need roughly 80 series to say much.

Now I'm working out whether 54 series is enough to detect the modest negative correlation I'd expect, and it looks underpowered; my rough calculation suggests around 80% power would need well over 100 series. I also want to flag that the adherence label may be tied to the outcome itself, since the recommendation could be built from points per possession, which moves with winning.

I'm settling on proceed_with_changes rather than running the study exactly as posed: pre-registering it, testing within series at the game level with team fixed effects, controlling for team quality, and fitting the recommendation on prior-season or out-of-sample data. I'm putting the outcome at roughly 12% supported, 5% rejected, 20% untestable, 20% artifact, and 43% uncertain. The four records get their statuses as given, with SF-CHT-039 and SF-APPA-027 as untestable and SF-APPS-017 and SF08 as not hypothesis tests.
